title: Rotate Image
description: Brute force to optimized: computing directly into a separate matrix versus decomposing the rotation into an in-place transpose followed by row-reversal.

blocks.text: Given an n x n 2D matrix representing an image, rotate the image by 90 degrees clockwise, IN PLACE (you must modify the input matrix directly, without allocating another full-size matrix).

blocks.caption: Transpose the matrix, then reverse each row, achieving the rotation in place

blocks.text: Given a square matrix, rotate it 90 degrees clockwise, modifying it directly without allocating a second full-size matrix to hold the result.

blocks.title: Analogy: Rotating a Photograph by Flipping It Twice
blocks.text: Like rotating a printed photograph 90 degrees clockwise using only two simpler physical motions: first, flip it over its top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal (as if folding along that line), then flip each row of the result left-to-right. Doing both motions in sequence, directly on the same physical photograph, achieves the full rotation without ever needing a second sheet of paper.

blocks.caption: A 90-degree clockwise rotation decomposes into transpose followed by row-reversal, both achievable in place

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Transpose: swap across the main diagonal, giving [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]","After transpose: [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]","Every matrix[i][j] and matrix[j][i] have been swapped"],["Reverse each row: [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]]","After row-reversal: [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]]","Reversing every row completes the 90-degree clockwise rotation"],["Answer","[[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]]","This matches rotating the original matrix 90 degrees clockwise"]]}

blocks.text: A single-element matrix is already its own rotation in every direction, so no transformation is actually needed, though the transpose-then-reverse steps trivially leave it unchanged anyway.

Before trying to directly compute each element's final rotated position and juggle in-place swaps for an unfamiliar transformation, notice that the rotation can be broken down into two much simpler, already-familiar operations.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Rotating 90 degrees clockwise moves the element at matrix[i][j] to position [j][n-1-i] in the final result.

Observation 2: This exact transformation can be achieved in two simpler steps: first TRANSPOSE the matrix (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for every i < j, moving element (i,j) to position (j,i)), then REVERSE every row (moving element (j,i) to position (j, n-1-i)).

Observation 3: Chaining these two steps together: (i,j) -> (j,i) via transpose -> (j, n-1-i) via row reversal, which is exactly the target rotated position.

Observation 4: Both the transpose and the row-reversal can each be performed in place, using simple swaps, so their combination achieves the full 90-degree rotation without ever needing a second full-size matrix.

Recognizing that a seemingly novel transformation (90-degree rotation) decomposes into two already-familiar, simpler in-place operations (transpose, then reverse) avoids needing to derive new in-place swap logic from scratch.
This is a decomposition technique: breaking an unfamiliar in-place transformation into a sequence of simpler, already-known in-place operations (here, Transpose Matrix followed by a row reversal).
Directly compute each element's final rotated position and place it into a separate result matrix, then copy the result back.

items: For every cell (i, j) in the original matrix, compute its final rotated position, (j, n-1-i), and place the value there in a separate result matrix.
Copy the fully computed result back into the original matrix, satisfying the in-place requirement only at this final step.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The rotated position formula (j, n-1-i) is applied directly to every cell, computed once per cell with no decomposition needed.
A full separate result matrix is used to avoid overwriting values that are still needed for later placements.
The final copy-back step is what nominally satisfies "in place", though the algorithm still uses O(n squared) auxiliary space internally.

blocks.text: Every element is placed directly into its correctly computed rotated position, so the result is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), visiting every cell exactly once.
Space: O(n squared) for the separate result matrix, which defeats the spirit of an in-place solution even though the final matrix ends up correct.

Limitation: using a full separate result matrix, even if copied back at the end, uses O(n squared) extra space, when the rotation can instead be decomposed into two operations that are each genuinely in-place.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force uses a full separate matrix internally. Instead, decompose the rotation into two truly in-place steps: first transpose the matrix by swapping matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for every i < j (touching only the upper triangle, to avoid swapping each pair twice), then reverse every row using a simple two-pointer swap. Both operations modify the matrix directly, using no auxiliary storage beyond a few temporary variables.

First, transpose the matrix in place: for every i from 0 to n-1 and every j from i+1 to n-1, swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]. Then, reverse every row in place, using a two-pointer swap from both ends moving inward.
Transpose the matrix in place, then reverse every row in place, achieving the full rotation with no extra full-size storage.

blocks.title: Final result
blocks.text: The matrix [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]] matches the expected 90-degree clockwise rotation.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), visiting each cell a constant number of times across both the transpose and reversal steps.
Space: O(1) extra, since both operations swap values directly within the existing matrix.

Transposing moves the element originally at (i, j) to position (j, i). Reversing each row afterward moves whatever sits at (row, col) to (row, n-1-col); applied to the transposed element now at (j, i), this moves it to (j, n-1-i), which is exactly the target position for a 90-degree clockwise rotation. Chaining these two independently-correct, independently-in-place operations therefore correctly achieves the full in-place rotation.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Transpose step (i < j)","Swap matrix[i][j] and matrix[j][i], touching each off-diagonal pair exactly once"],["Row-reversal step","Each row is reversed independently using a standard two-pointer swap"]]}

items: The transpose loop only considers j > i, ensuring each pair of symmetric positions is swapped exactly once (not swapped back by a later iteration).
The diagonal (i == j) is never touched during transpose, since a cell always stays in place relative to itself.
Row reversal is applied to every row independently after the transpose is fully complete, ensuring no partial state interference between the two steps.

blocks.text: Decomposing an unfamiliar in-place transformation into a sequence of simpler, already-known in-place operations (here, transpose then row-reversal) is a broadly reusable strategy whenever a direct in-place approach isn't immediately obvious.

items: Swapping the full matrix during transpose (including j < i), which would swap every pair back to its original position, undoing the transpose entirely.
Reversing rows BEFORE transposing instead of after, which produces a counter-clockwise rotation instead of clockwise (or requires transposing along the opposite diagonal to compensate).
Allocating a full separate matrix "just to be safe", missing the actual in-place requirement the problem explicitly asks for.

items: State the transpose-then-reverse decomposition explicitly and verify it algebraically ((i,j) -> (j,i) -> (j, n-1-i)) before coding, since deriving and confirming this exact position mapping is what an interviewer is specifically checking for.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Rotate a matrix 90 degrees IN PLACE" points toward decomposing the rotation into transpose (swap across the diagonal) followed by reversing every row, both individually in-place operations.

items: How would you rotate 90 degrees COUNTER-clockwise instead? Either transpose then reverse every COLUMN (instead of every row), or reverse every row first and then transpose, achieving the mirrored decomposition.
How would you rotate 180 degrees? Reverse every row AND reverse the overall row order (or equivalently, apply the 90-degree rotation twice), achieving a full half-turn.

What if the matrix were very large and stored on disk (not fully in memory)? The transpose step would need careful block-wise or tiled processing to minimize disk I/O, since naive element-by-element transposition could be prohibitively slow for out-of-memory data.
Directly builds on Transpose Matrix (an earlier problem in this same category), decomposing this more complex in-place rotation into that already-solved sub-problem plus a simple row-reversal step.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n squared) space.
Optimized (transpose + reverse rows, in place): O(n squared) time, O(1) extra space.

items: Pattern: Decomposing an in-place transformation into simpler, already-known in-place operations (transpose, then row-reversal)
Core Idea: A 90-degree clockwise rotation is exactly equivalent to transposing the matrix, then reversing every row
Time: O(n squared)
Space: O(1) extra
Most Important Observation: An unfamiliar in-place transformation can often be decomposed into a sequence of simpler, already-solved in-place operations
Interview Difficulty: Medium
One-line memory trick: Rotate 90 degrees clockwise = transpose, then reverse every row
